name: Justified True Belief
statement: To know something is to have a belief that is both true and justified: the classical analysis of knowledge.
statementAccent: a belief that is both true and justified
meaning: Justified true belief, often abbreviated JTB, is the traditional or classical analysis of what it is to know a proposition, to have knowledge that something is the case, as opposed to knowing how to do something. It holds that knowledge consists of three conditions, each individually necessary and together jointly sufficient. A subject S knows that a proposition p is the case if and only if, first, p is true, since one cannot know a falsehood; second, S believes that p, since one cannot know what one does not even believe; and third, S is justified in believing that p, meaning the belief is adequately supported by good evidence or reasoning rather than being a mere lucky guess. The account is usually traced back to Plato's dialogue the Theaetetus, where an early version of the idea that knowledge is more than mere true opinion is explored, though the strict three-part formula is a modern reconstruction rather than a doctrine Plato states in that form. For much of the twentieth century the JTB analysis was the standard reference point in the theory of knowledge, the definition that epistemologists took as their starting point. In 1963 Edmund Gettier published a short paper presenting counterexamples showing that the three conditions can all be met while intuitively no knowledge is present, and JTB is now widely regarded as necessary but not sufficient for knowledge.
mechanism: The JTB analysis breaks knowing that p into three separate conditions and claims that meeting all three is exactly what knowledge is. The truth condition requires that p actually be true; a belief in a falsehood, however confident or well-supported, is not knowledge, because knowledge is factive. The belief condition requires that the subject actually believe p; one cannot be said to know something one does not believe, so knowledge presupposes belief. The justification condition requires that the subject's belief be justified, that is, appropriately supported by evidence, reasons, or reliable grounds, so as to rule out lucky guesses and beliefs held for no good reason; true belief that happens to be right by accident, like a correct hunch, is not knowledge. These three conditions are held to be individually necessary, so that dropping any one leaves something short of knowledge, and jointly sufficient, so that meeting all three amounts to knowledge. The analysis thus treats knowledge as a compound of a mental state, belief, a worldly fact, truth, and a normative epistemic relation, justification. Its great use was to make the concept of knowledge tractable by decomposing it, and to focus attention on justification as the ingredient that turns mere true belief into knowledge. Edmund Gettier's 1963 counterexamples work by constructing cases in which a belief is justified and true, yet true only by luck in a way that disconnects the justification from the truth, so that the belief satisfies JTB but is not knowledge, showing the three conditions are not jointly sufficient.

examples.text: To know that p, on the JTB analysis, p must be true, you must believe p, and you must be justified in believing p.
A correct hunch is a true belief but not knowledge, because the justification condition demands good grounds, not luck.
Gettier's 1963 cases meet all three JTB conditions yet are not knowledge, since the belief is true only by luck.

variants.name: The tripartite analysis
variants.text: Knowledge as belief that satisfies the three conditions of truth, belief, and justification, each necessary and jointly sufficient.

variants.name: Post-Gettier repairs
variants.text: Attempts to add or modify a fourth condition, such as no false lemmas, reliability, or defeasibility, to fix JTB.

whyItMatters: Justified true belief is the central starting point of the modern theory of knowledge, the definition against which nearly all later work in epistemology defines itself. By analyzing knowledge into the three conditions of truth, belief, and justification, it gave the concept a clear and tractable structure and identified justification as the crucial ingredient that separates genuine knowledge from mere true belief or lucky guessing. For much of the twentieth century the JTB account was simply the received view of what knowledge is. Its importance only grew when Edmund Gettier's 1963 paper, Is Justified True Belief Knowledge?, showed with a few short counterexamples that the three conditions can be satisfied without knowledge being present, launching an enormous literature, the analysis of knowledge project, devoted to diagnosing what JTB leaves out and to proposing a fourth condition or a replacement. Whether the response is to add a no-false-lemmas clause, to require reliability, to demand that the justification be undefeated, or to abandon the project of analysis altogether, the debate takes JTB as its point of departure. As the classical analysis of knowledge and the target of the Gettier problem, justified true belief remains foundational to epistemology.

working.text: insist that p be true, since knowledge is factive and one cannot know a falsehood.
insist that the subject actually believe p, since knowledge presupposes belief.
insist that the belief be adequately supported by evidence or reasoning, ruling out lucky guesses.

limits: The JTB analysis is now widely held to be necessary but not sufficient for knowledge, the key limitation exposed by the Gettier problem. In 1963 Edmund Gettier gave short counterexamples in which a subject has a belief that is justified and true, yet true only through luck in a way that severs the connection between the justification and the truth, so that we do not count it as knowledge even though all three JTB conditions are met. This showed that truth, belief, and justification are not jointly sufficient. A large literature has since tried to repair the account, by adding a fourth condition such as that the reasoning involve no false lemmas, that the belief be produced by a reliable process, or that the justification be undefeated by further truths, but no single repair commands universal agreement, and some conclude that knowledge cannot be analyzed into simpler conditions at all. The Plato attribution should also be hedged, since the Theaetetus explores knowledge as true belief with an account rather than stating the modern three-part formula. So the JTB analysis robustly captures much of what knowledge requires, understood as the classical account that Gettier showed to be necessary but not sufficient.
misreadings: Justified true belief is not an uncontroversially correct definition of knowledge; Gettier's counterexamples show the three conditions can be met without knowledge, so JTB is necessary but not sufficient. It is not a doctrine Plato stated in the modern three-part form, since the Theaetetus explores an early version rather than the strict formula. And satisfying it is not the same as certainty, since the justification condition allows for fallible justification, so treating JTB as the settled definition, as Plato's own tripartite theory, or as a guarantee of certainty, misreads the classical analysis that the Gettier problem undermined.
origin: The classical analysis of propositional knowledge as belief that is both true and justified, with the three conditions individually necessary and jointly sufficient, traced to Plato's Theaetetus and shown insufficient by Edmund Gettier in 1963.

sources.text: The Analysis of Knowledge, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — the justified-true-belief analysis as holding that knowledge is justified true belief, the three conditions of truth, belief, and justification as individually necessary and jointly sufficient, the roots in Plato's Theaetetus, and the Gettier problem showing the conditions insufficient.

The Gettier Problem, Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — the traditional JTB account of knowledge, the requirement that a justified belief be well supported rather than a lucky guess, and Gettier's 1963 counterexamples refuting the sufficiency of JTB.
